claim: Stimulation of RKO cells with IFNγ strongly induced endogenous IRF1 protein levels by 11.2-fold.
source: Stimulation of RKO cells with IFNγ strongly induced endogenous IRF1 protein levels (Figure 1A; 11.2-fold).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A with a specific quantification of 11.2-fold induction.

claim: IRF1 levels returned to pre-stimulation protein levels within 4 hr in the absence of de novo protein synthesis.
source: In the absence of de novo protein synthesis, IRF1 levels returned to pre-stimulation protein levels within 4 hr, indicating that it is highly unstable.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cycloheximide chase experiments.

claim: IRF1 is highly unstable.
source: In the absence of de novo protein synthesis, IRF1 levels returned to pre-stimulation protein levels within 4 hr, indicating that it is highly unstable.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rapid depletion of IRF1 protein within 4 hours.

claim: Inhibition of lysosomal degradation by Bafilomycin A did not affect endogenous IRF1 stability and half-life.
source: Simultaneous inhibition of lysosomal degradation by Bafilomycin A (Baf) did not affect endogenous IRF1 stability and half-life (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B), indicating that IRF1 is predominantly turned over by the proteasome.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: IRF1 is predominantly turned over by the proteasome.
source: Simultaneous inhibition of lysosomal degradation by Bafilomycin A (Baf) did not affect endogenous IRF1 stability and half-life (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B), indicating that IRF1 is predominantly turned over by the proteasome.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of lysosomal inhibition and the effect of proteasome inhibition on IRF1 levels.

claim: Inhibition of proteasomal degradation by MG132 increased IRF1 levels.
source: In line with this finding, endogenous IRF1 protein levels measured by intracellular staining were also induced by IFNγ and depleted upon translation inhibition (Figure 1B; left panel), whereas inhibition of proteasomal degradation by MG132 increased IRF1 levels (Figure 1B; right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IRF1 is induced by IFNγ and degraded by the proteasome in RKO cells.
source: Together, these results indicate that IRF1 is induced by IFNγ and degraded by the proteasome in RKO cells, as has been described for other cell types, making it a suitable model for identification of IRF1 stability regulators.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental observations including IFNγ induction and proteasome inhibitor effects.

claim: RKO cells are a suitable model for identification of IRF1 stability regulators.
source: Together, these results indicate that IRF1 is induced by IFNγ and degraded by the proteasome in RKO cells, as has been described for other cell types, making it a suitable model for identification of IRF1 stability regulators.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RKO cells exhibit expected IRF1 behavior.

claim: The half-life of endogenous IRF1 is 72 min.
source: Single exponential decay curve fitting indicated the half-life of endogenous IRF1 to be 72 min, whereas the half-life of mCherry-IRF1 was twice as long at 144 min (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of protein decay curves shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The half-life of mCherry-IRF1 is 144 min.
source: Single exponential decay curve fitting indicated the half-life of endogenous IRF1 to be 72 min, whereas the half-life of mCherry-IRF1 was twice as long at 144 min (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of protein decay curves shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The half-life of mCherry-cMYC is 24 min.
source: Similar measurements for mCherry-cMYC indicated a 24 min half-life for mCherry-cMYC and 19 min for endogenous cMYC in the same cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D), consistent with previously published work (Welcker et al., 2004; Yada et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The half-life of endogenous cMYC is 19 min.
source: Similar measurements for mCherry-cMYC indicated a 24 min half-life for mCherry-cMYC and 19 min for endogenous cMYC in the same cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D), consistent with previously published work (Welcker et al., 2004; Yada et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: cMYC has a 20–30 min half-life.
source: cMYC is constantly turned over by the proteasome with a 20–30 min half-life (Gregory and Hann, 2000; Ramsay et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mCherry-cMYC screen strongly identified FBXW7 in mCherry-cMYChigh cells.
source: As anticipated, the mCherry-cMYC screen strongly identified its well-known degrader FBXW7 in mCherry-cMYChigh cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by screen data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: FBXW7 is a well-known degrader of cMYC.
source: As anticipated, the mCherry-cMYC screen strongly identified its well-known degrader FBXW7 in mCherry-cMYChigh cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge referenced in the context.

claim: The mCherry-cMYC screen identified proteasome components PSMC5, PSMD4, and PSMD11.
source: Moreover, it identified other UPS components reported to mediate cMYC degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), such as proteasome components (PSMC5, PSMD4, PSMD11), the proteasome regulator AKIRIN2 (de Almeida et al., 2021), and the UPS-related ATPase VCP/p97 (Heidelberger et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by screen data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: AKIRIN2 is a proteasome regulator.
source: Moreover, it identified other UPS components reported to mediate cMYC degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), such as proteasome components (PSMC5, PSMD4, PSMD11), the proteasome regulator AKIRIN2 (de Almeida et al., 2021), and the UPS-related ATPase VCP/p97 (Heidelberger et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: VCP/p97 is a UPS-related ATPase.
source: Moreover, it identified other UPS components reported to mediate cMYC degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), such as proteasome components (PSMC5, PSMD4, PSMD11), the proteasome regulator AKIRIN2 (de Almeida et al., 2021), and the UPS-related ATPase VCP/p97 (Heidelberger et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The mCherry-IRF1 screen identified 27 high confidence factors which specifically affected mCherry-IRF1 abundance.
source: The mCherry-IRF1 screen identified 27 high confidence factors which specifically affected mCherry-IRF1 abundance, but neither mCherry-cMYC nor the stable BFP controls (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by screen data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: SPOP was the only candidate strongly enriched at both 3 and 6 days after Cas9 induction in the mCherry-IRF1 screen.
source: The only candidate strongly enriched at both 3 and 6 days after Cas9 induction was the Cullin E3 ligase receptor speckle type BTB/POZ protein (SPOP), which did not score in the mCherry-cMYC screen (Figure 2B–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by screen data shown in Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: SPOP did not score in the mCherry-cMYC screen.
source: The only candidate strongly enriched at both 3 and 6 days after Cas9 induction was the Cullin E3 ligase receptor speckle type BTB/POZ protein (SPOP), which did not score in the mCherry-cMYC screen (Figure 2B–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by screen data shown in Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: Seven nuclear transport-related factors (NUP35, NUP85, NUP93, NUP155, NUP160, TMEM48, NUTF2) were identified in the mCherry-IRF1 screen.
source: In addition, seven nuclear transport-related factors (NUP35, NUP85, NUP93, NUP155, NUP160, TMEM48, NUTF2) were identified (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that nuclear translocation of IRF1 or one of its degraders may be important for its degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by screen data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Nuclear translocation of IRF1 or one of its degraders may be important for its degradation.
source: In addition, seven nuclear transport-related factors (NUP35, NUP85, NUP93, NUP155, NUP160, TMEM48, NUTF2) were identified (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that nuclear translocation of IRF1 or one of its degraders may be important for its degradation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the identification of nuclear transport factors in the screen.

claim: SPOP has been previously reported to localize to the nucleus and degrade nuclear substrates.
source: Consistent with this notion, SPOP has been previously reported to localize to the nucleus and degrade nuclear substrates (Marzahn et al., 2016; Usher et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: FBXW7, MDM2, and STUB1/CHIP did not score as significant IRF1 regulators in the screen.
source: Previously described regulators of IRF1 proteasomal turnover such as FBXW7, MDM2, or STUB1/CHIP (Garvin et al., 2019; Landré et al., 2013; Narayan et al., 2011b) did not score as significant IRF1 regulators in our screen, indicating that they are unlikely to play a significant role in IRF1 degradation in this cellular context, although we cannot rule out that unknown technical aspects in the screen prevented their identification.
evidence: The claim is supported by screen data and references to previously published literature.

claim: FBXW7, MDM2, and STUB1/CHIP are unlikely to play a significant role in IRF1 degradation in RKO cells.
source: Previously described regulators of IRF1 proteasomal turnover such as FBXW7, MDM2, or STUB1/CHIP (Garvin et al., 2019; Landré et al., 2013; Narayan et al., 2011b) did not score as significant IRF1 regulators in our screen, indicating that they are unlikely to play a significant role in IRF1 degradation in this cellular context, although we cannot rule out that unknown technical aspects in the screen prevented their identification.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of identification in the screen, with acknowledgment of potential technical limitations.

claim: Ablation of SPOP specifically increased the abundance of mCherry-IRF1.
source: Ablation of top-scoring putative regulators of cMYC (FBXW7, UBE3C, VCP) substantially increased mCherry-cMYC levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), whereas targeting SPOP specifically increased the abundance of mCherry-IRF1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SPOP ablation increased endogenous IRF1 levels by 40%.
source: Consistent with our screen data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), SPOP ablation increased endogenous IRF1 levels by 40%, whereas endogenous cMYC protein levels were not affected (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SPOP ablation did not affect endogenous cMYC protein levels.
source: Consistent with our screen data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), SPOP ablation increased endogenous IRF1 levels by 40%, whereas endogenous cMYC protein levels were not affected (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All seven different sgRNAs targeting SPOP significantly increased IRF1 levels compared to controls.
source: All seven different sgRNAs significantly increased IRF1 levels compared to the two independent controls, indicating that specific SPOP targeting underlies this phenotype, and not off-target effects (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Specific SPOP targeting underlies the IRF1 stabilization phenotype, not off-target effects.
source: All seven different sgRNAs significantly increased IRF1 levels compared to the two independent controls, indicating that specific SPOP targeting underlies this phenotype, and not off-target effects (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the consistency of effects across multiple independent sgRNAs.

claim: Western blot analysis of three independent monoclonal SPOP knockout cell lines showed that IRF1 levels were increased by 50–70%.
source: Consistent with this notion, western blot analysis of three independent monoclonal SPOP knockout cell lines showed that IRF1 levels were increased by 50–70% (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: SPOP ablation specifically affected IRF1 protein levels, as IRF1 mRNA concentrations were not significantly changed in SPOP knockout cells.
source: This effect of SPOP ablation specifically affected IRF1 protein levels, as IRF1 mRNA concentrations were not significantly changed in SPOP knockout cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: SPOP ablation in mouse embryonic fibroblasts increased endogenous IRF1 protein levels.
source: In line with our results from human cell lines, SPOP ablation in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) likewise increased endogenous IRF1 protein levels (Figure 3G–H), indicating a conserved mechanism across species and non-transformed cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claim: SPOP-mediated IRF1 regulation is a conserved mechanism across species and non-transformed cell types.
source: In line with our results from human cell lines, SPOP ablation in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) likewise increased endogenous IRF1 protein levels (Figure 3G–H), indicating a conserved mechanism across species and non-transformed cell types.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of similar effects in both human and mouse cells.

claim: SPOP is important for regulating IRF1 protein levels, without affecting its mRNA concentrations.
source: In summary, these findings demonstrate that SPOP is important for regulating IRF1 protein levels, without affecting its mRNA concentrations.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Both IRF1 and SPOP localized in the nucleoplasm.
source: Consistent with previous reports, both IRF1 and SPOP localized in the nucleoplasm (Figure 4A), indicating that they are present in the same subcellular compartment, and thus could interact.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SPOP was also present at nuclear speckles.
source: While both proteins localized dispersedly in the nucleoplasm, in both tested cell types SPOP was also present at nuclear speckles, as previously described (Marzahn et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data and citation to published literature.

claim: IRF1 and SPOP are present in the same subcellular compartment and thus could interact.
source: Consistent with previous reports, both IRF1 and SPOP localized in the nucleoplasm (Figure 4A), indicating that they are present in the same subcellular compartment, and thus could interact.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of co-localization in the nucleoplasm.

claim: Proteasome inhibitor treatment increased the diffuse nucleoplasmic IRF1 signal.
source: Under these conditions, the diffuse nucleoplasmic IRF1 signal increased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that this represents the unstable cellular IRF1 pool.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The diffuse nucleoplasmic IRF1 signal represents the unstable cellular IRF1 pool.
source: Under these conditions, the diffuse nucleoplasmic IRF1 signal increased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that this represents the unstable cellular IRF1 pool.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the increase in signal upon proteasome inhibition.

claim: In the presence of proteasome inhibitor, the SPOP puncta increased in size and signal intensity.
source: Moreover, in the presence of proteasome inhibitor, the SPOP puncta increased in size and signal intensity, consistent with previous reports that these are sites of SPOP-dependent degradation of a subset of its targets (Marzahn et al., 2016; Usher et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations and citations to published literature.

claim: SPOP puncta are sites of SPOP-dependent degradation of a subset of its targets.
source: Moreover, in the presence of proteasome inhibitor, the SPOP puncta increased in size and signal intensity, consistent with previous reports that these are sites of SPOP-dependent degradation of a subset of its targets (Marzahn et al., 2016; Usher et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: None of the IRF1 signal was detected in the SPOP puncta.
source: However, none of the IRF1 signal was detected in the SPOP puncta (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IRF1 is likely targeted for degradation in the nucleoplasm.
source: Together, these data suggest that IRF1 is likely targeted for degradation in the nucleoplasm, and that this could potentially be mediated by the diffuse nucleoplasmic SPOP pool.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from localization data.

claim: IRF1 degradation could potentially be mediated by the diffuse nucleoplasmic SPOP pool.
source: Together, these data suggest that IRF1 is likely targeted for degradation in the nucleoplasm, and that this could potentially be mediated by the diffuse nucleoplasmic SPOP pool.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from localization data.

claim: IFNγ treatment rapidly induced IRF1 in the nuclear fraction.
source: Consistent with our microscopy results (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), IFNγ treatment rapidly induced IRF1 in the nuclear fraction, which even further increased upon SPOP depletion (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Nuclear IRF1 levels further increased upon SPOP depletion.
source: Consistent with our microscopy results (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), IFNγ treatment rapidly induced IRF1 in the nuclear fraction, which even further increased upon SPOP depletion (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: SPOP targets IRF1 in the nucleus, where it is subsequently degraded.
source: These data reinforce the conclusion that SPOP targets IRF1 in the nucleus, where it is subsequently degraded.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: SPOP has an S/T-rich binding consensus of [Φ]-[Π]-[S]-[S/T]-[S/T], in which Φ and Π are non-polar and polar residues, respectively.
source: Previous studies had identified an S/T-rich SPOP binding consensus of [Φ]-[Π]-[S]-[S/T]-[S/T], in which Φ and Π are non-polar and polar residues, respectively (Zhuang et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Four sequences in IRF1 match the SPOP degron consensus.
source: A multiple sequence alignment of IRF1 across species (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) identified four sequences in IRF1 matching the SPOP degron consensus (Figure 4C), consistent with predictions (ScanProsite – Expasy, and Hou et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4C, and is consistent with computational predictions.

claim: One of the putative SPOP degrons was identified in the region between the DNA-binding domain and the IAD2 domain.
source: One of the putative SPOP degrons was identified in the region between the DNA-binding domain and the IAD2 domain, whereas the remaining three were predicted to be inside the IAD2 domain, which is important for transactivation and dimerization (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Three putative SPOP degrons were predicted to be inside the IAD2 domain.
source: One of the putative SPOP degrons was identified in the region between the DNA-binding domain and the IAD2 domain, whereas the remaining three were predicted to be inside the IAD2 domain, which is important for transactivation and dimerization (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The IAD2 domain is important for transactivation and dimerization.
source: One of the putative SPOP degrons was identified in the region between the DNA-binding domain and the IAD2 domain, whereas the remaining three were predicted to be inside the IAD2 domain, which is important for transactivation and dimerization (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the IAD2 domain.

claim: SPOP expression decreased wtIRF1 protein levels in a dose-dependent manner.
source: SPOP expression decreased wtIRF1 protein levels in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4D), without affecting the stable EGFP internal control.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SPOP expression did not affect the stable EGFP internal control.
source: SPOP expression decreased wtIRF1 protein levels in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4D), without affecting the stable EGFP internal control.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Protein levels of the IRF1 degron mutant remained unaffected by exogenous SPOP expression.
source: In contrast, protein levels of the IRF1 degron mutant remained unaffected by exogenous SPOP expression, suggesting that one or more of the four predicted degrons are required for SPOP-dependent IRF1 degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and mutant IRF1.

claim: One or more of the four predicted degrons are required for SPOP-dependent IRF1 degradation.
source: In contrast, protein levels of the IRF1 degron mutant remained unaffected by exogenous SPOP expression, suggesting that one or more of the four predicted degrons are required for SPOP-dependent IRF1 degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutating the degrons prevents SPOP-dependent degradation.

claim: SPOP immunoprecipitation identified wtIRF1, but not IRF1-SBDmut.
source: Subsequent western blot analysis for IRF1 identified wtIRF1, but not IRF1-SBDmut (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of wtIRF1 identified SPOP, but not when IRF1-SBDmut was immunoprecipitated.
source: The reciprocal approach in which wtIRF1 or IRF1-SBDmut were immunoprecipitated, exclusively identified SPOP upon purification of wtIRF1, but not its degron mutant (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SPOP interaction with S/T degrons has been previously mapped to its MATH domain.
source: SPOP interaction with S/T degrons has been previously mapped to its MATH domain (Zhuang et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: wtIRF1 interacted with wtSPOP, yet failed to co-immunoprecipitate MATH-domain mutated SPOP.
source: In line with this observation, wtIRF1 interacted with wtSPOP, yet failed to co-immunoprecipitate MATH-domain mutated SPOP (SPOP-MATHmut) (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The reciprocal pull-down of wtSPOP identified wtIRF1, whereas the SPOP mutant showed strongly reduced interaction with IRF1.
source: Consistently, the reciprocal pull-down of wtSPOP identified wtIRF1, whereas the SPOP mutant showed strongly reduced interaction with IRF1 (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: IRF1 ubiquitination was significantly increased upon co-expression of wtSPOP, but not with MATH-domain mutated SPOP.
source: In line with one or more of the four identified degrons being important for SPOP-dependent IRF1 turnover, IRF1 ubiquitination was significantly increased upon co-expression of wtSPOP, but not with MATH-domain mutated SPOP (SPOP-MATHmut).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data.

claim: Upon mutation of the SPOP binding sequences, IRF1 ubiquitination was significantly decreased.
source: Upon mutation of the SPOP binding sequences, IRF1 ubiquitination was significantly decreased (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4I–J.

claim: Some or all of the SPOP degrons are required for IRF1 poly-ubiquitination.
source: From this, we concluded that some or all of the SPOP degrons are required for IRF1 poly-ubiquitination, although the remaining ubiquitination in the IRF1 mutant indicates that additional E3 ligases may ubiquitinate IRF1 as well.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion inferred from ubiquitination assay data.

claim: Additional E3 ligases may ubiquitinate IRF1.
source: From this, we concluded that some or all of the SPOP degrons are required for IRF1 poly-ubiquitination, although the remaining ubiquitination in the IRF1 mutant indicates that additional E3 ligases may ubiquitinate IRF1 as well.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation of residual ubiquitination in the degron mutant.

claim: Mutation of all lysines in the N-terminal half of the DNA-binding domain (DBD1), its C-terminal half (DBD2), the NLS region, or its C-terminal domain (C-term.) did not alter IRF1 sensitivity to treatment with proteasome inhibitor.
source: Mutation of all lysines in the N-terminal half of the DNA-binding domain (DBD1), its C-terminal half (DBD2), the NLS region, or its C-terminal domain (C-term.) did not alter its sensitivity to treatment with proteasome inhibitor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: An IRF1 mutant in which all lysines were mutated in the entire IRF1 protein (allKtoR) was no longer stabilized by proteasome inhibition.
source: In contrast, an IRF1 mutant in which all lysines were mutated in the entire IRF1 protein (allKtoR) was no longer stabilized by proteasome inhibition, suggesting that SPOP targets lysines in multiple IRF1 domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing lysine mutants.

claim: SPOP targets lysines in multiple IRF1 domains.
source: In contrast, an IRF1 mutant in which all lysines were mutated in the entire IRF1 protein (allKtoR) was no longer stabilized by proteasome inhibition, suggesting that SPOP targets lysines in multiple IRF1 domains.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only mutation of all lysines prevents stabilization.

claim: Expression of wtSPOP in AAVS1-targeted RKO cells did not alter endogenous IRF1 protein concentrations compared to an empty vector control.
source: Expression of wtSPOP in AAVS1-targeted RKO cells did not alter endogenous IRF1 protein concentrations compared to an empty vector control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, left panel), indicating that SPOP levels in these cells were likely not limiting for IRF1 turnover.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: SPOP levels in AAVS1-targeted RKO cells were likely not limiting for IRF1 turnover.
source: Expression of wtSPOP in AAVS1-targeted RKO cells did not alter endogenous IRF1 protein concentrations compared to an empty vector control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, left panel), indicating that SPOP levels in these cells were likely not limiting for IRF1 turnover.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of exogenous SPOP expression.

claim: The elevated IRF1 protein levels in SPOP KO cells were decreased by exogenous wtSPOP expression to levels measured in wild-type cells.
source: In contrast, the elevated IRF1 protein levels in SPOP KO cells were decreased by exogenous wtSPOP expression to levels measured in wild-type cells, whereas they were not affected by the empty vector control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H; middle panel and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: IRF1 levels were only rescued by wtSPOP expression, but not by its MATH domain mutant counterpart.
source: Consistent with our interaction data and requirement of the SPOP MATH domain for IRF1 targeting (Figure 4G–H), IRF1 levels were only rescued by wtSPOP expression, but not by its MATH domain mutant counterpart (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: IRF1 is targeted by SPOP for ubiquitination through interaction of the SPOP MATH domain with S/T-rich degrons in IRF1, resulting in subsequent IRF1 degradation.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that IRF1 is targeted by SPOP for ubiquitination through interaction of the SPOP MATH domain with S/T-rich degrons in IRF1, resulting in subsequent IRF1 degradation.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: IRF1 is required for efficient transcription of interferon-induced genes (ISGs).
source: IRF1 is required for efficient transcription of interferon-induced genes (ISGs).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about IRF1 function.

claim: IRF1 is important for transcriptional induction of a subset of ISGs, such as members of the guanylate binding protein (GBP) family in response to IFNs.
source: IRF1 is in particular important for transcriptional induction of a subset of ISGs, such as members of the guanylate binding protein (GBP) family in response to IFNs (Ramsauer et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: GBP2, GBP3, and IFIT3 are putatively IRF1-dependent immune effector ISGs in RKO cells.
source: By querying the harmonizome project for IRF1 transcriptional targets (Rouillard et al., 2016), we identified the ISGs GBP2, GBP3, and IFIT3 as putatively IRF1-dependent immune effector ISGs, and PARP14 and APOL2 as IRF1-dependent non-immune effector genes in RKO cells.
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis of transcriptional target databases.

claim: PARP14 and APOL2 are IRF1-dependent non-immune effector genes in RKO cells.
source: By querying the harmonizome project for IRF1 transcriptional targets (Rouillard et al., 2016), we identified the ISGs GBP2, GBP3, and IFIT3 as putatively IRF1-dependent immune effector ISGs, and PARP14 and APOL2 as IRF1-dependent non-immune effector genes in RKO cells.
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis of transcriptional target databases.

claim: SPOP ablation did not significantly change the mRNA concentration of IRF1 independently transcribed NLRC5.
source: As expected, SPOP ablation did not significantly change the mRNA concentration of IRF1 independently transcribed NLRC5 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SPOP ablation significantly increased the mRNA levels of IRF1-dependent immune-related targets GBP2, GBP3, and IFIT3.
source: In contrast, SPOP ablation significantly increased the mRNA levels of IRF1-dependent immune-related targets GBP2, GBP3, and IFIT3 (Figure 5A) in the presence of IRF1.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of GBP2, GBP3, and IFIT3 was reduced to equal levels in both IRF1 and IRF1/SPOP knockout cells.
source: Expression was reduced to equal levels in both IRF1 and IRF1/SPOP knockout cells, indicating that differences in ISG expression in SPOP KO cells are dependent on IRF1-driven transcription.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data comparing different knockout conditions.
